# The Four Big Risks - Accountability Breakdown

**Article:** "The Four Big Risks" by Marty Cagan, December 4, 2017

**The Four Risks and Accountability:**

"1. _value_ risk (whether customers will buy it or users will choose to use it)
2. _usability_ risk (whether users can figure out how to use it)
3. _feasibility_ risk (whether our engineers can build what we need with the time, skills and technology we have)
4. _business viability_ risk (whether this solution also works for the various aspects of our business)"

**Role Accountability:**

"The **Product Manager** is responsible for the _value_ and _viability_ risks, and overall accountable for the product's _**outcomes**_."

"The **Product Designer** is responsible for the _usability_ risk, and overall accountable for the product's _**experience**_ – every interaction our users and customers have with our product."

"The **Product** **Lead Engineer** is responsible for the _feasibility_ risk, and overall accountable for the product's _**delivery**_."

# Product Trio: Key Passages

**Source:** "Core Concept: The Product Trio" by Teresa Torres, 05 May 2021

---

1. **Definition:** "A product trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a software engineer."

2. **Core Roles:** "These are the three roles that—at a minimum—are required to create good digital products."

3. **Traditional Problems:** "This model is rife with challenges. Oftentimes, the product manager doesn't know what's possible and the engineers can't implement the requirements as written."

4. **Team Motivation:** "Great products tend to be built by missionary teams. A missionary team needs to have a say in what they are building."

5. **Shared Understanding:** "When a product trio works together to develop a shared understanding of their customer, they are in a much better position to create products that customers love."

6. **Collaborative Process:** "They work collaboratively from beginning to end, iterating their way to their desired outcome."

7. **Decision-Making:** "They [interview customers together]. They [map out the opportunity space together]. They choose a [target opportunity] together."

8. **Impact:** "When product managers, designers, and engineers work together as product trios, they have more impact."

# The Definition of User Experience (UX)
**By Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen**
**August 8, 1998**

## Full Definition of UX

"User experience" encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products."

## Distinguishing Passages

1. "The first requirement for an exemplary user experience is to meet the exact needs of the customer, without fuss or bother."

2. "It's important to distinguish the total user experience from the user interface (UI), even though the UI is obviously an extremely important part of the design."

3. "Even if the UI for finding a film is perfect, the UX will be poor for a user who wants information about a small independent release if the underlying database only contains movies from the major studios."

4. "We should also distinguish UX and usability: According to the definition of usability, it is a quality attribute of the UI, covering whether the system is easy to learn, efficient to use, pleasant, and so forth."

5. "Again, this is very important, and again total user experience is an even broader concept."

# User Experience Analysis (UNAN)

**Skill Code:** UNAN

**Overall Description:** "Understanding the context of use for systems, products and services and specifying user experience requirements and design goals."

**Guidance Notes:**
"This skill is inclusive of a full range of user tasks not just digital tasks. The skill can be applied in various contexts, such as: customer experience, products, services, applications, devices, learning experience and employee experience."

Activities include: "identifying, analysing, clarifying and communicating the context in which the product or service will be used" and "describing users' goals, tasks and the environment within which the systems, products, services or devices will be used."

**Level 3 (Apply):**
"Applies standard techniques and tools for developing user stories and eliciting user experience requirements. Organises and structures user experience analysis. Works with stakeholders to prioritise requirements and resolve conflicts."

**Level 4 (Enable):**
"Selects appropriate techniques and tools to develop user stories and elicit user experience requirements in complex situations. Identifies and describes the design goals for systems, products, services and devices."

**Level 5 (Ensure, advise):**

## Product Designer & Product Manager Failure Modes

### Design by Committee

Design by committee is an unfavorable process involving too many parties participating in the product design decision-making process, resulting in a less effective platform for the users. If you treat every piece of feedback equally and every opinion as truth, you may end up with a bloated, Frankenstein-esque product--a loosely stitched together mashup of various opinions and ideas.

Most design by committee projects fall apart in one of three predictable ways. You end up with a bloated, disjointed "Frankenstein" design that tries to please everyone and fails at all of it. Strong product vision dies in committee.

A prominent example is the Pontiac Aztek: General Motors wanted to import some Procter & Gamble-style innovation and let focus groups drive the concept development while also letting many different internal groups chime in. The resulting product was a commercial failure. Sales of the Pontiac Aztek reached only a fraction of what was predicted, and the vehicle never reached profitability.

### Pixel Pusher

A lot of people forget that designer is more than just a pixel pusher. When you look deeper into design, you will understand that behind the overall goal of design is problem solving. Design is about solving user problems and running business objectives.

If your organization views design this way, then you will continue to receive aesthetic and superficial feedback — becoming that truly dreaded term 'pixel pusher'.

### Product Management Theater

The reason this is described as "product management theater" is because a person that is essentially a project manager, with no real training or skills to cover the true product management responsibilities, simply declaring they are a product manager, is just pretending.

"Fake" product managers engage in non-essential activities, often under titles like Agile coaches, product owners, product operations, or business analysts. During the pandemic, tech companies hired excessively for product roles, leading to a surplus of ineffective product managers who now resemble overpaid project managers.

When product owners or business analysts are re-titled to product managers. Or when graphic designers are re-titled to product designers. This "title theater" represents a common failure mode where roles change names but not competencies.

Based on the Nielsen Norman Group content, here's what I found about Product Designer vs UX Designer:

## Key Differences

"Product designer" is an increasingly common catch-all term for UX designers who have broad expertise in research and design skills, with a particular area of specialty. Product designers hold responsibility for ensuring that products address real user needs and are usable.

Product designers usually have a keen awareness of business strategy, as they should be able to connect design improvements with business impact.

## Job Title Inconsistency

NN/G research highlights a broader challenge with UX job titles: 2019 survey respondents reported 134 unique job titles related to UX (slightly down from the 210 job titles reported in 2013, but still far from any agreement on job titles). The term "user experience" (in full) winning over prefixes like 'product', 'digital', 'human factors', or 'usability.'

## Practical Takeaway

There have never been clearly standardized, consistent labels for job roles in UX. (Anyone who has looked for a UX designer role will be familiar with how important it is to doublecheck the job description and not rely on the title alone, lest they accidentally end up working as a front-end developer.)

In summary, "Product Designer" is a broad, modern term that encompasses UX designers with diverse expertise, but the exact responsibilities vary significantly by organization.

# Design by Committee: Key Passages

**1. Definition:**
"Design by committee is what happens when multiple parties are involved in the product design process, and all of their input is treated equally."

**2. Core Problem:**
"The problem is not with the feedback itself but with how the product team chooses to act."

**3. Consequences:**
"By the time it was done, it came out as this horrible, least-common-denominator vehicle where everyone said, 'How could you put that on the road?'"

**4. Lack of Single Owner:**
"Committee design is not collaborative. It's a dictatorship of many, and you'll be reduced to implementer rather than facilitator."

**5. Need for Centralized Decision-Making:**
"Product should be a dictatorship. Not consensus-driven. There are casualties. Hurt feelings. Angry users. But all of those things are necessary if you're going to create something unique."

**6. Authority and Empowerment:**
"When they know the end product will achieve the initial goals not by chance but because of thoughtful research and careful consideration of every decision, they'll be less inclined to worry about the details."

"The biggest disagreement was related to discoveries" with only 19% of PMs versus 73% of UXers believing UX should own this work.

"More than three quarters of UX respondents" thought ideation was UX's job, "but only about a third of the PM respondents" agreed, with another third assigning it to PM.

"76% of UX respondents" believed explaining design to leadership was UX's responsibility, yet "45% of PM respondents" thought PM should handle this task.

## Vision & Prioritization
"More than 63%" of PMs considered vision and business prioritization their job, while "UXers were usually split between assigning these tasks to product owners."

## Design Execution
PMs appropriated wireframing and task-flow definition tasks despite UXers believing these belonged to design professionals.

The article references Marty Cagan's concept of "empowered teams," where designers own solving usability risks—contrasting with typical "feature teams" requiring more PM specification.

6. **On collaborative wireframing:**
"The Wireframes Contract" establishes ground rules allowing PMs to create wireframes alongside designers, emphasizing two separate sets rather than PMs dictating final designs.

# Design by Committee: Key Passages

**Title:** Design By Committee: Definition, Examples & Reasons To Avoid It  
**Author:** Jen Lee (Reviewer)  
**Date:** Last updated 16 April 2023

---

**Definition:**
"Design by committee is a form of democratic teamwork. It involves a group of designers, stakeholders, and clients working on the same project and sharing equally valid opinions."

**Why It Fails:**
"In product design, it usually produces low-quality results" when compromises emerge from unstructured teams lacking data-driven decisions and established processes.

**The Problem:**
"Discussion without collaboration" occurs because "design by committee involves doing the guesswork without qualitative and quantitative data to validate hypotheses."

**The Solution:**
"While you can have a large team of designers, you should only have one decision-maker. Your entire team should understand that no matter how valuable their opinions and decisions seem, only one person makes the final call."

**Collaborative Alternative:**
"In collaborative design, the teams are structured between departments, with a decision-maker implementing needs based on validated qualitative and quantitative data centered on user feedback."

## C. Cross-source observations for the writer
1. Decision right (high confidence — Cagan 2017, 2025; NN/g RACI): the designer is accountable for usability risk / the experience across every interaction; PM for value+viability; engineer for feasibility. Discovery is joint (Torres), accountability single (NN/g RACI).
2. Scope (high): UX ⊃ UI ⊃ usability (Norman & Nielsen); "all touchpoints and interactions" (Cagan 2016); interaction design = "conversation between the user and the system" (Cagan & Baxley 2025) — medium-neutral, so CLI/API/agent are in scope by definition. No opened source addresses CLI/API explicitly (that's SQ3/SQ4).
3. Evidence the role admits (high): prototypes, user tests/trials, expert review, context-of-use analysis, generative research (Cagan 2016; SFIA HCEV/USEV/URCH; ISO 9241-210 activities via secondary).
4. Contested boundary with PM (high, NN/g 2021 survey): discovery research, ideation, IA, task flows, research agenda, explaining design to leadership. Definition should allocate each explicitly.
5. Failure modes with sources: PM-supplied wireframes to "polish" (NN/g 2023); PM "waded into the design waters" (Cagan 2006); designer as decorator/pixel-pusher (Marvel 2018); design by committee / unowned equal input (ProductPlan, Dovetail); waterfall hand-off leaving designer to find requirement gaps (Torres 2024); title-only "product designer" (NN/g title proliferation). "Design theater" — unsupported by any opened source.
6. Unopened: ISO 9241-210 text (paywalled); NN/g "UX vs product designer" (403); NHS blog (403); NN/g careers PDF (not fetched).
